interest: This document provides a concise official summary of the legal status of foreign land ownership in Japan under the Alien Land Law of 1925 (effective November 10, 1926). It is historically significant for showing how the Japanese Government approached reciprocal property rights in response to foreign—most notably American state-level (e.g., California)—alien land laws that barred Japanese nationals from owning land. It documents that despite statutory authority to impose retaliatory restrictions via Imperial Ordinance, Japan exercised restraint and refrained from implementing reciprocal bans against American and other foreign nationals.
overview: This file contains a Department of State informational memorandum prepared in April 1938 regarding the Alien Land Law of Japan (Law No. 42 of 1925, effective November 10, 1926). The memorandum summarizes the legal provisions governing real property acquisition by foreign nationals, explaining that while aliens are granted equal ownership rights with Japanese subjects, the law contains a reciprocal clause permitting restrictions by Imperial Ordinance against nationals of countries that restrict land ownership by Japanese citizens. It notes that the Japanese Government had publicly disclaimed any immediate intention to enforce this reciprocal restriction and that no restrictive Imperial Ordinances had been enacted.

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing the provisions and practical application of the Japanese Alien Land Law of 1925 regarding foreign ownership of real property.
subfiles.summary: This memorandum examines the status of real property ownership by foreigners under Japan's Alien Land Law (Law No. 42 of 1925), which entered into force on November 10, 1926. While establishing equal landownership rights for aliens, the statute includes a qualifying provision allowing the government to prohibit or restrict ownership via Imperial Ordinance for nationals of jurisdictions that prohibit or restrict Japanese landholding. The note records that the Japanese Government announced upon implementation that it did not intend to apply this qualifying clause for the time being, and confirms that no such restrictive Imperial Ordinances had yet been promulgated as of April 1938.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Alien Land Law of Japan
